title: Data Newsroom
tagline: You ask questions of a table of data. Then you decide if a headline is true.
objectives: Write a rule with a column, a sign and a number or a word, and read how many rows it keeps.
Join two rules with AND, which needs both, or OR, which needs one.
Use BETWEEN to keep every number from one end to the other, both ends in.
Use NOT to keep the rows a rule would leave out.
Say whether the numbers back a headline, and if not, why: too few people, only the best bit, the numbers say no, one did not cause the other.

opening.line1: You will check if headlines are telling the truth.
opening.line2: Posts, adverts and the news are not always true.

story.b1: Fionn, our reporter, went home sick.
story.b2: Check his six headlines before midnight.
story.b3: PRINT the true ones. SPIKE the rest. SPIKE means you throw the headline in the bin.

facts.intro: Fionn’s facts are in two tables. Each table has rows and columns.
facts.t1: Table one: 60 people of Rathmore answered a survey.
facts.t2: Table two: 92 summer days at the harbour.

tour.s1: This is the table. Each row is one person.
tour.s2: Type a rule in this box. The table keeps only rows that fit.
tour.s3: This is the count. It shows how many rows are left.

c1.title: The question
c1.headline: Eight hours of sleep lifts exam scores
c1.show1: A rule has a column, a sign and a number.
c1.show2: < means less than, so this keeps people under 20.
c1.ask: Keep only the people who slept eight hours or more.
c1.h1: The column is sleep_hours. Eight or more is >=.

judge.ok: Right. 17 people. A rule like this is a query.
judge.wrong: Your rule keeps {got} rows, not 17. Check the sign.

options: No. The people who slept eight hours or more scored lower.
c1.right: Right. The numbers say the opposite.
c1.wrong: No. People who slept eight or more hours scored lower than others, not higher.
c1.stampShow2: Dee stamped it SPIKE: do not print.
c1.stampAsk: Your turn now. Stamp the sleep headline.
c1.stampOk: SPIKE. Those who slept eight hours or more scored lower, not higher.
c1.stampNo: Look at the two averages. Which group scored higher?
c1.reasonNo: Seventeen people is enough. The averages say no.
c1.doneLine: You have done one headline. Five are left.
c1.stampShowCard: Harbour café is the town favourite

c2.title: Two at once
c2.headline: Most Rathmore teens are on their phones five hours a day
c2.show1: AND keeps rows where both rules are true.
c2.show2: Here: teens who have a dog.
c2.show3: Words go in quotes. Numbers do not.
c2.ask: Keep teens who use their phone five hours or more.
c2.h1: For teens, use age < 20. For five hours or more, use phone_hours >= 5.
c2.h2: Put AND between the two rules.

judge.ok: Right. 6 of the 18 teens use their phone that much.
judge.wrong: Your rule keeps {got} rows, not 6. Check both rules.

c2.right: Right. Six of eighteen is one in three.
c2.wrong: Six of eighteen is one in three. One in three is not most.
c2.stampOk: SPIKE. The numbers say no: 6 of 18 is not most.
c2.stampNo: Six of the 18 teens use their phone five hours or more. Is that most of them?
c2.reasonNo: Eighteen teens is enough. The problem is the word "most".
c2.doneLine: You have done two headlines. Four are left.
c2.luck: Your rule keeps the right 6 rows, but it never checks for teens. Add AND and a rule on age.
c2.wrongOr: Your rule keeps {got} rows, not 6. OR keeps rows where either rule is true. Use AND.
c2.wrongOne: Your rule keeps {got} rows, not 6. Add AND and a second rule.

c3.title: One week
c3.headline: Rathmore harbour gets 3,000 visitors a day
c3.show1: BETWEEN keeps every number from the first to the second.
c3.show2: Here: summer days at 20, 21 or 22 degrees.
c3.ask: Fionn only looked at days 40 to 46. Keep those days.
c3.h2: Write day_no, then BETWEEN, then the first day, then AND, then the last day.

judge.ok: Right. Your rule keeps 7 days. Those days are regatta week, the week of the boat races.
judge.wrong: Your rule keeps {got} days, not 7. Check both ends.

c3.compare1: Those 7 days had 3,158 visitors a day.
c3.compare2: All 92 days had 2,215 visitors a day.
options: Took the best week and called it the summer.
He did nothing wrong. 3,000 is the right number.
c3.right: Right. One good week is not the whole summer.
c3.wrong: He took the best week. All 92 days had only 2,215 visitors a day.
c3.stampOk: SPIKE. Fionn used only the best week. Regatta week is not the whole summer.
c3.stampNo: Can seven days show the whole summer?
c3.reasonNo: Those seven days are real, but they were the best week of the summer.
c3.doneLine: You have done three headlines. Three are left.

c4.title: Either one
c4.headline: More than half of Rathmore people have a dog or a cat
c4.show1: OR keeps rows where either rule is true.
c4.show2: Here: people in Marsh or Hill.
c4.show3: Write the column name on both sides of OR.
c4.ask: Keep everyone with a dog or a cat.
c4.h1: The column is pet. Words go in quotes: "dog".
c4.h2: Type pet = "dog" OR pet = "cat". Each side is a full rule.

judge.ok: Right. 31 people have a dog or a cat.
judge.wrong: Your rule keeps {got} rows, not 31. Write the column name on both sides of OR.

c4.wrong: Thirty-one of sixty is over half. This one is true.
c4.stampOk: PRINT. The numbers back it: 31 of 60.
c4.stampNo: 31 of 60 is over half. Is it true?
c4.reasonNo: This one is true. Why do you print it?
c4.doneLine: You have done four headlines. Two are left.
c4.wrongAnd: Your rule keeps {got} rows, not 31. AND keeps rows where both rules are true. Use OR.
c4.wrongOne: Your rule keeps {got} rows, not 31. Use OR to keep dogs and cats.

c5.title: Leave out
c5.headline: Outside Old Town, everyone loves the new bus
c5.show1: NOT flips a rule. It keeps the rows the rule throws out.
c5.ask: Keep people outside Old Town who gave the bus any stars.
c5.h1: You need two rules: one for Old Town and one for the stars. Put NOT at the start of the Old Town rule.

judge.wrong: Your rule keeps {got} rows. Look at the part about stars. Giving any stars means giving more than 0 stars.

c5.compare2: The other 40 people outside Old Town did not rate the bus.
c5.right: Right. Four people cannot tell us what all 44 think.
c5.wrong: Four people rated it. They cannot tell us what all 44 think.
c5.stampOk: SPIKE. The reason is too few people. Only 4 of the 44 people outside Old Town rated the bus.
c5.stampNo: Just 4 of 44 rated the bus. Is that everyone?
c5.reasonNo: The four did love it. But four is too few.
c5.doneLine: You have done five headlines. One is left.
c5.wrongNot: Your rule keeps {got} rows. Put NOT before area.
c5.wrongAnd: Your rule keeps {got} rows. Add AND and a rule for the stars.

c6.title: The rush
c6.headline: Ice cream sales cause sea rescues
c6.ring: One headline is left. The printing press starts in three minutes. If time runs out, the press prints Fionn’s headline.
c6.intro: Check hot days, then cold days.
c6.ask1: Keep the hot days: 24 degrees or more.

judge1.ok: Right. An average hot day had 290 ice creams sold and 2.8 sea rescues.
judge1.wrong: Your rule keeps {got} days, not 27. Check the sign.

c6.ask2: Now keep the days under 18 degrees.

judge2.ok: Right. An average cold day had 91 ice creams sold and 0.5 sea rescues.
judge2.wrong: Your rule keeps {got} days, not 28. Check the sign.

c6.stampAsk: Be quick. Stamp the headline now.
c6.stampOk: SPIKE. Ice cream did not cause the rescues. Hot weather caused the sales and the rescues.
c6.stampNo: Sales and rescues both rise on hot days. What causes both?
c6.reasonNo: The numbers are real. But could something else cause both the ice cream sales and the sea rescues?
c6.timeUp: It is midnight. Time ran out.
c6.printedLine: The press printed Fionn’s headline on page one.
c6.letter1: Dear Editor, I sell ice cream. My ice cream does not cause sea rescues.
c6.letter2: Hot weather causes both the sales and the rescues.
c6.fixOk: You fixed it. The heat caused the sales and the rescues.
c6.compare1: Hot days averaged 290 ice creams and 2.8 rescues a day.
c6.compare2: Cold days averaged 91 ice creams and 0.5 rescues a day.

recap: AND keeps rows where both rules are true. OR keeps rows where either rule is true.
BETWEEN keeps the first number, the last number and every number in between.
NOT goes before a rule. It keeps the rows that the rule would throw out.
Check the numbers before you print.

items.head: Hill people go to the café less than everyone else
items.ask: Keep the people who live in Hill.

items.head: Fish owners are the café’s best customers
items.ask: Keep the people who own a fish.
items.ok: SPIKE. Only {n} people own a fish. That is too few people to trust the average.

items.head: Harbour people are older than everyone else
items.ask: Keep the people who live in Harbour.
card: These {n} people are {a:age} years old on average.
items.ok: PRINT. Harbour people average {a:age} years. Everyone else averages {r:age}.

items.head: Teenagers sleep less than adults
items.ask: Keep the people under 20.
card: These {n} teens sleep {a:sleep_hours} hours a night on average.
items.ok: SPIKE. Teens sleep {a:sleep_hours} hours a night and adults sleep {r:sleep_hours} hours. Teens sleep more, not less.

items.head: Wet days have fewer visitors
items.ask: Keep the days with more than 5 mm of rain.
items.ok: PRINT. Wet days average {a:visitors} visitors. Other days average {r:visitors}.

items.head: A scorching summer: 30 degrees at the harbour
items.ask: Keep the days of 30 degrees or more.
items.ok: SPIKE. Just {n} day hit 30 degrees. The rest averaged {r:temp_c}.

items.head: Old Town people use their phones more than everyone else

items.ok: PRINT. Old Town averages {a:phone_hours} hours. Everyone else averages {r:phone_hours}.

items.head: Living in Old Town makes you use your phone more

card: These {n} people use their phones {a:phone_hours} hours a day. The rest average {r:phone_hours}.
These {n} people are {a:age} years old on average. The rest average {r:age}.
items.no: Look at the ages of the Old Town people. Could their age explain how much they use their phones?
items.ok: SPIKE. All the Old Town people are teenagers. Their age explains the phone use, not the place they live.

items.head: July was the busiest month at the harbour
items.ask: Keep the days in July.
items.ok: PRINT. July averaged {a:visitors} visitors, more than June or August.

items.head: August was the driest month
items.ask: Keep the days in August.
card: August days average {a:rain_mm} mm of rain.
June averaged {x:rain_mm:june} mm. July averaged {x:rain_mm:july} mm.

items.head: Cat owners are older than everyone else

card: These {n} people are {a:age} years old on average.
items.ok: PRINT. Cat owners average {a:age} years. Everyone else averages {r:age}.

card: These {n} pet owners average {a:cafe_visits} café visits.
items.ok: SPIKE. Pet owners average {a:cafe_visits} café visits. Everyone else averages {r:cafe_visits}. The two numbers are almost the same. Pet owners do not visit far more.

items.head: Hot days bring the biggest crowds
items.ask: Keep the days of 24 degrees or more.
items.ok: PRINT. Hot days average {a:visitors} visitors. Other days average {r:visitors}.

items.ok: SPIKE. Wet days had fewer rescues, not more.

why.sign: That rule uses {ws}, which means {wm}. The question needs {rs}, which means {rm}.
why.col: That rule looks in the {wc} column. The question needs the {rc} column.
why.value: That rule uses {wv}. The question needs {rv}.
why.needAnd: OR keeps rows where at least one part is true. The question needs both parts true, so use AND.
why.needOr: AND keeps only rows where both parts are true. The question wants rows where either part is true, so use OR.
why.noNot: That rule has no NOT, so it keeps the rows the question leaves out.
why.notWrong: NOT keeps the rows that do not fit the rule. This question wants the rows that do fit it.
why.outside: That rule keeps the rows outside {a} to {b}.
why.ends: BETWEEN keeps the first number and the last number too. The signs > and < leave those two numbers out.

items.facts: The table has 9 dog owners and 22 cat owners.
items.why: OR keeps both groups: 9 + 22 = 31.

items.facts: The table has 9 dog owners and 22 cat owners.
items.why: No one’s pet is a dog and a cat at once.

items.facts: The table has 60 people. 22 of them own a cat.
items.why: NOT keeps everyone else: 60 − 22 = 38.

items.facts: 4 people are under 16. 7 people are exactly 16.
items.why: The sign <= keeps people under 16 and people who are exactly 16. So the count is 4 + 7 = 11.

items.facts: 4 people are under 16. 7 people are exactly 16.
items.why: The sign < leaves out the 7 people who are exactly 16. So it keeps only the 4 people under 16.
BETWEEN keeps both the first and the last day. Day 10 and day 20 both count. So days 10 to 20 make 11 days.
Only days 91 and 92 are over 90.

items.facts: June has 30 days. July and August have 31 each.
items.why: OR keeps both months: 30 + 31 = 61.

items.facts: June has 30 days. July and August have 31 each.
items.why: NOT keeps June and July: 92 − 31 = 61.

items.facts: June has 30 days. July and August have 31 each.
items.why: No day is in two months at once.

items.facts: 16 people live in Old Town. 15 live in Hill.
items.why: OR keeps both areas: 16 + 15 = 31.

items.facts: The table has 60 people. 16 live in Old Town.
items.why: NOT keeps everyone else: 60 − 16 = 44.

items.facts: All 16 Old Town people are teens. There are 18 teens.
items.why: Every Old Town person is a teen, so all 16 stay.

items.facts: The table has 60 people. 25 have no pet.
items.why: NOT keeps the pet owners: 60 − 25 = 35.
No one is over 100, so no rows are left.
BETWEEN keeps both ends: days 1 to 30 is 30 days.
